fields.Front: When should you choose a SQL (relational) database over NoSQL?
fields.Back: When you need strong consistency, complex multi-table joins/transactions, and a fixed, well-understood schema.

fields.Front: When should you choose a NoSQL database over SQL?
fields.Back: When you need horizontal scalability, a flexible/evolving schema, and can relax strict consistency (e.g. massive write throughput, unstructured data).

fields.Front: What is a key-value store best suited for? Give an example.
fields.Back: Simple lookups by a unique key with no query complexity, e.g. Redis for caching or session storage.

fields.Front: What is a document store best suited for? Give an example.
fields.Back: Semi-structured, nested data accessed as whole records, e.g. MongoDB for product catalogs or user profiles.

fields.Front: What is a column-family (wide-column) store best suited for? Give an example.
fields.Back: Very high write throughput and queries over huge, sparse datasets, e.g. Cassandra for time-series or logging data.

fields.Front: What is a graph database best suited for? Give an example.
fields.Back: Data where relationships/traversals matter more than the entities themselves, e.g. Neo4j for social networks or recommendation engines.

fields.Front: What data structure do most relational database indexes use, and why?
fields.Back: A B-tree, because it keeps data sorted and supports O(log n) lookups, range scans, and ordered traversal at balanced depth.

fields.Front: Why does adding an index speed up reads?
fields.Back: It lets the DB search a sorted structure instead of scanning every row, turning an O(n) full scan into an O(log n) lookup.

fields.Front: What is the write-side cost of adding an index?
fields.Back: Every insert/update/delete must also update the index structure, which slows writes and uses extra storage.
Organizing data into related tables to eliminate redundancy, using foreign keys instead of duplicating data.

fields.Front: What is database denormalization, and why is it used at scale?
fields.Back: Deliberately duplicating data across tables/documents to avoid expensive joins, trading storage and write complexity for faster reads.

fields.Front: What problem do read replicas solve?
fields.Back: They offload read traffic from the primary/leader database by serving reads from copies, scaling read throughput.

fields.Front: What is a downside of read replicas?
fields.Back: Replication lag can cause a replica to serve stale (slightly outdated) data compared to the primary.

fields.Front: What problem does connection pooling solve?
fields.Back: It reuses a fixed set of already-open DB connections across requests instead of opening/closing a new connection per request, avoiding costly connection-setup overhead and exhausting the DB's connection limit.

fields.Front: Why store large binary files (images, videos) in blob/object storage (e.g. S3) instead of a database?
fields.Back: Databases are optimized for structured, queryable records, not large binaries; object storage is cheaper, scales better, and offloads that load from the DB.

fields.Front: What kind of data is a time-series database (e.g. InfluxDB) optimized for?
fields.Back: Data points indexed by time, like metrics or sensor readings, with efficient time-range queries and aggregation/downsampling.

fields.Front: What is Elasticsearch typically used for in a system design?
fields.Back: Full-text search and complex filtering/ranking over large datasets, using an inverted index — usually alongside, not instead of, a primary data store.

fields.Text: The four main NoSQL families are {{c1::key-value}}, {{c2::document}}, {{c3::column-family (wide-column)}}, and {{c4::graph}} stores.
Indexing speeds up {{c1::reads}} (faster lookups via a sorted structure) but slows down {{c2::writes}} (every index must be updated on each write).

fields.Back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the transaction guarantees of traditional relational (SQL) databases.
